correctness.rationale: Exact derivative identity integrates over ordered disjoint incidence-drop intervals. H>=0 produces the budget. Gaussian pulses in the negative log-transmission derivative yield a strictly decreasing real analytic beta with total drop < epsilon and log derivative magnitude < 5. Uniform S and I bounds imply H in [2867/2125,13/5] and beta S>1. Pulse centers give negative d log incidence/dt, inter-pulse midpoints positive, guaranteeing k strict alternating extrema while I increases. Prescribed narrow Gaussian pulse masses make the sum of peak-to-trough logarithmic drops converge to the total beta log drop, proving constant one sharp. Verified rational margins and sampled integrations with the packaged script; finite experiments are not proof of unrestricted quantifiers.

originality.rationale: The motivating source already establishes the basic logarithmic incidence identity and arbitrarily many peaks for unrestricted transmission. The claimed combined contribution adds the sharp global logarithmic peak-depth budget (constant achieved asymptotically) and a constructive all-k analytic decreasing-transmission family with arbitrarily small total log drop, uniform first log-slope bound and increasing infectious prevalence. Full primary-text comparisons and actual focused searches found no stronger theorem covering this constrained combination. The elementary integrated budget alone is not characterized as novel. Relevant inverse and Gaussian-forcing precedents are explicitly delimited, and unindexed overlap remains a risk.
residual_risks: Related inequality could have been derived as an unlabelled direct corollary of the known incidence identity.
Unindexed epidemic observability or variation-budget literature may contain a stronger all-k or sharpness theorem under different terminology.
The numerical examples do not verify an infinite claim; the proof uses exact comparisons and Gaussian asymptotics.

value.rationale: The result addresses a concrete mathematical gap in interpreting peak topology in time-varying epidemic models: raw strict incidence peak count is arbitrarily unstable under monotone analytic forcing with bounded first log slope and vanishing net variation, yet aggregate log peak prominence obeys a sharp budget. This dichotomy provides quantitative mathematical support for minimum-prominence/model-resolution criteria rather than merely restating the known incidence-extremum identity. Scientific scope excludes clinical interpretation and robust high-prominence wave generation.
